data.title: Companies Like Upland Resources (LON:UPL) Can Afford To Invest In Growth
data.description:
Just because a business does not make any money, does not mean that the stock will go down. For example, biotech and mining exploration companies often lose money for years before finding success with a new treatment or mineral discovery. But while the successes are well known, investors should not ignore the very many unprofitable companies that simply burn through all their cash and collapse.

So, the natural question for Upland Resources (LON:UPL) shareholders is whether they should be concerned by its rate of cash burn. In this report, we will consider the company's annual negative free cash flow, henceforth referring to it as the 'cash burn'. The first step is to compare its cash burn with its cash reserves, to give us its 'cash runway'.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

Does Upland Resources Have A Long Cash Runway?

A cash runway is defined as the length of time it would take a company to run out of money if it kept spending at its current rate of cash burn. In June 2026, Upland Resources had UK£2.7m in cash, and was debt-free. Looking at the last year, the company burnt through UK£674k. Therefore, from June 2026 it had 4.0 years of cash runway. A runway of this length affords the company the time and space it needs to develop the business. Depicted below, you can see how its cash holdings have changed over time.

View our latest analysis for Upland Resources

How Is Upland Resources' Cash Burn Changing Over Time?

Because Upland Resources isn't currently generating revenue, we consider it an early-stage business. Nonetheless, we can still examine its cash burn trajectory as part of our assessment of its cash burn situation. From a cash flow perspective, it's great to see the company's cash burn dropped by 86% over the last year. While that hardly points to growth potential, it does at least suggest the company is trying to survive. Upland Resources makes us a little nervous due to its lack of substantial operating revenue. We prefer most of the stocks on this list of stocks that analysts expect to grow.

How Easily Can Upland Resources Raise Cash?

There's no doubt Upland Resources' rapidly reducing cash burn brings comfort, but even if it's only hypothetical, it's always worth asking how easily it could raise more money to fund further growth. Generally speaking, a listed business can raise new cash through issuing shares or taking on debt. One of the main advantages held by publicly listed companies is that they can sell shares to investors to raise cash and fund growth. By looking at a company's cash burn relative to its market capitalisation, we gain insight on how much shareholders would be diluted if the company needed to raise enough cash to cover another year's cash burn.

Upland Resources' cash burn of UK£674k is about 1.5% of its UK£45m market capitalisation. That means it could easily issue a few shares to fund more growth, and might well be in a position to borrow cheaply.

So, Should We Worry About Upland Resources' Cash Burn?

As you can probably tell by now, we're not too worried about Upland Resources' cash burn. In particular, we think its cash burn reduction stands out as evidence that the company is well on top of its spending. And even its cash burn relative to its market cap was very encouraging. After taking into account the various metrics mentioned in this report, we're pretty comfortable with how the company is spending its cash, as it seems on track to meet its needs over the medium term. On another note, Upland Resources has 3 warning signs (and 2 which are concerning) we think you should know about.

data.title: We Think U10's (EPA:ALU10) Solid Earnings Are Understated
data.description:
U10 Corp (EPA:ALU10) announced a healthy earnings result recently, and the market rewarded it with a strong uplift in the stock price. Looking deeper at the numbers, we found several encouraging factors beyond the headline profit numbers.

This technology could replace computers: discover the 20 stocks are working to make quantum computing a reality.

Zooming In On U10's Earnings

One key financial ratio used to measure how well a company converts its profit to free cash flow (FCF) is the accrual ratio. To get the accrual ratio we first subtract FCF from profit for a period, and then divide that number by the average operating assets for the period. The ratio shows us how much a company's profit exceeds its FCF.

That means a negative accrual ratio is a good thing, because it shows that the company is bringing in more free cash flow than its profit would suggest. While having an accrual ratio above zero is of little concern, we do think it's worth noting when a company has a relatively high accrual ratio. To quote a 2014 paper by Lewellen and Resutek, "firms with higher accruals tend to be less profitable in the future".

U10 has an accrual ratio of -0.21 for the year to June 2026. That indicates that its free cash flow quite significantly exceeded its statutory profit. Indeed, in the last twelve months it reported free cash flow of €14m, well over the €2.40m it reported in profit. Notably, U10 had negative free cash flow last year, so the €14m it produced this year was a welcome improvement.

That might leave you wondering what analysts are forecasting in terms of future profitability. Luckily, you can click here to see an interactive graph depicting future profitability, based on their estimates.

Our Take On U10's Profit Performance

Happily for shareholders, U10 produced plenty of free cash flow to back up its statutory profit numbers. Because of this, we think U10's underlying earnings potential is as good as, or possibly even better, than the statutory profit makes it seem! And it's also positive that the company showed enough improvement to book a profit this year, after losing money last year. Of course, we've only just scratched the surface when it comes to analysing its earnings; one could also consider margins, forecast growth, and return on investment, among other factors. data.title: How Stronger Revenue Will Impact Con Edison (ED) Investors
data.description:
• Consolidated Edison reported third quarter 2026 revenue of US$4.91b and net income of US$766m, with basic EPS from continuing operations at US$2.07, all above the prior year period.
  • The utility paired this higher year to date profit with plans for about US$797m of climate resilience spending through 2030, linking recent earnings strength to long term infrastructure hardening.
  • We will now look at how Consolidated Edison’s stronger revenue performance fits into its existing investment narrative and how it may influence that narrative over time.

Scan how Consolidated Edison's earnings story compares with other regulated utilities by reviewing our hand picked list of 42 power grid technology and infrastructure stocks.

Consolidated Edison Investment Narrative Recap

For a shareholder in Consolidated Edison, the core belief is that a tightly regulated utility can keep turning heavy grid and resilience spending into dependable earnings. The latest quarter delivered higher revenue and net income year on year, which supports that thesis. The near term swing factor is still how regulators treat returns on this growing rate base, and this update does not materially change that.

The biggest operational worry remains stress during extreme weather and the cost of preventing or fixing outages. Higher nine month profit gives management some room to fund climate and reliability projects, but large capital needs, debt coverage and free cash flow pressure stay front of mind for anyone watching the balance sheet.

The most relevant recent announcement is Consolidated Edison’s plan for about US$797m of climate resilience investment from 2026 to 2030. That sits on top of a much larger long term grid program and directly links to the rate base growth many investors focus on. It also targets the same reliability issues that showed up during the 2026 heat waves.

This resilience plan interacts closely with the current earnings story. Stronger operating results in 2026 help support a heavier capital program, while regulators decide how much of that spending goes into rates and allowed returns. For you, the key question is whether this combination of higher capital intensity, debt funding needs and regulatory oversight still lines up with your view of Consolidated Edison’s risk and reward profile.

Analyst Expectations Behind the Consolidated Edison Story

Analysts are effectively sketching a steady, regulated glide path for Consolidated Edison. Their models assume revenue grows by 3.5% a year over the next few years while profit margins lift from 12.5% today to 14.2% by 2029. That set up points to earnings moving from about US$2.2b today to a consensus forecast of roughly US$2.8b by 2029, an increase of about US$600m that depends heavily on regulators allowing returns on a larger rate base.

Those same forecasts feed directly into how the stock is currently framed. To line up with the analyst view, you would need to accept that by 2029 Consolidated Edison generates about US$19.6b of revenue and US$2.8b of profit, with the shares trading around 18.9x those earnings. The implied future P/E sits a little below the current US integrated utilities industry level quoted in the report, which suggests the group of analysts see the stock as reasonably priced rather than a clear outlier on either value or risk.

Consolidated Edison's narrative projects about US$19.6b revenue and US$2.8b earnings by 2029. This requires 3.5% yearly revenue growth and an earnings increase of roughly US$600m from current earnings of about US$2.2b.
